headline: A rough day across the board — the ASX fell 1.6% and US markets tanked last night, dragging most of your holdings lower, while GTA VI's monster $3.79B day-one result gives Take-Two a rare bright spot.

movers.name: Global X AI ETF
movers.note: Biggest faller in the portfolio today. The AI ETF tracks global AI-related stocks, which copped a hammering last night on the NASDAQ (down 5.3%). When US tech sneezes, this ETF catches a cold hard — it's entirely exposed to that sector.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: A rare green day — Pilbara rose 2.3% today, bucking the broader market sell-off. Sentiment around lithium is ticking up slightly as traders focus on low Chinese stockpile levels, which could signal a demand pickup down the track. Still deeply underwater overall, but a positive session.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market ETF
movers.note: Fell 2.8% today as the ASX-listed fund repriced to reflect last night's brutal US session — the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% and the NASDAQ fell 5.3%. This ETF mirrors the whole US market, so it took the full hit.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 2.8% last night in a broad tech sell-off that hit the NASDAQ hard. No specific Microsoft news drove the fall — the whole sector was under pressure. The long-term story around Microsoft's AI and cloud dominance remains intact.

movers.name: Alphabet (Google)
movers.note: Google fell 2.6% last night as part of the wider NASDAQ rout. Adding to the picture locally, Google has cancelled funding for 25 Australian news outlets under the News Media Bargaining Code — a reputational story but not a material financial one for the company.

movers.name: Vanguard Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: Dropped 2.4% today. Emerging markets took a hit from the strong risk-off mood globally — investors pulled back from higher-risk assets including developing markets. Taiwan's AI stock rout (the government had to ban short-selling to stabilise markets) would have added pressure.

movers.name: DHHF (Diversified High Growth ETF)
movers.note: Fell 2.3% today, tracking the broader global market weakness. DHHF holds a mix of international and Australian shares, so it felt the drag from both the US sell-off and the softer ASX session today.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: Down 2.1% today — same story as DHHF. A diversified high-growth fund with heavy international exposure will always reflect global market swings. Nothing structurally changed today; this is the cost of being exposed to growth assets.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: The only US holding to end in the green last night — up 0.65% — and for good reason. Take-Two revealed GTA VI generated a staggering $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, with day-one copies already exceeding the Nintendo 64's entire lifetime unit sales. This is a monster result that validates the long-term investment thesis.

watch_today.title: GTA VI day-one sales: $3.79 billion — TTWO thesis confirmed
watch_today.detail: Take-Two just reported GTA VI did $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales — one of the biggest entertainment launches in history. For a long-term holder, this is exactly what you bought TTWO for. The stock is still slightly underwater overall (-2.7%) but this result materially de-risks the position. Sit tight and let it run.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX down 4% — worst day-mover in the portfolio
watch_today.detail: The AI ETF copped a 4% hit today, its biggest single-session drop in the portfolio. This was driven by last night's NASDAQ crash (down 5.3%) which crushed global AI and tech stocks broadly. If you believe in the long-term AI growth story — and the launch of Google's Gemini 4 Neon and ongoing AI investment suggest you should — this is noise, not a reason to sell. Consider it a cheaper entry point if you're looking to top up.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX: a rare green day — but stay patient
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals popped 2.3% today as lithium sentiment gets a small lift from low Chinese stockpile data. It's still down 61% from your cost base, but the narrative is slowly shifting. Hold for the long term — the lithium recovery thesis takes time, and nothing has fundamentally changed.

watch_today.title: NASDAQ crashed 5.3% last night — broad US tech pain
watch_today.detail: The NASDAQ fell 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% last night — a significant risk-off session. This dragged VTS.AX, MSFT, GOOG, GXAI.AX and VDHG all lower today. US markets open tonight around 11:30 PM AEST — watch to see if there's a bounce or further selling. No single catastrophic event caused the fall; it appears to be broad macro pressure.

watch_today.title: RBA under scrutiny — rate debate intensifying
watch_today.detail: Multiple news outlets today are questioning whether the RBA has overtightened, with new unemployment data raising alarm bells. A divided RBA board suggests rates could move either way. This matters for your ASX holdings — if the RBA cuts, it's generally good for Aussie shares and growth assets like VDHG and DHHF.

watch_today.title: Iran attacks civilian site in Bahrain — Middle East tension rising
watch_today.detail: Iran struck a civilian industrial facility in Bahrain today, injuring two people. With oil prices already up slightly ($83.41/barrel), any further escalation could push energy costs higher globally — which feeds through to inflation and potentially delays rate cuts worldwide. Watch this space.

world.summary: The Middle East remains the dominant global flashpoint today, with Iran escalating its attacks beyond traditional borders. Meanwhile, the AI arms race heats up with a major new Google launch, and Taiwan takes emergency stock market action.

stories.title: Iran strikes civilian industrial facility in Bahrain, two injured
stories.why_it_matters: Iran launched an attack on a civilian industrial site in Bahrain on the weekend, causing a fire and injuring two people. This marks a significant escalation — Iran is now targeting Gulf Arab states beyond its traditional adversaries. For everyday people, this matters because the Persian Gulf is the world's main oil shipping corridor. Any serious escalation risks spiking global oil prices, pushing up fuel costs and inflation everywhere, including here on the Gold Coast.

stories.title: Iran's missile ambitions now extend beyond the Middle East
stories.why_it_matters: An analysis piece in Al-Monitor reveals that years of regional conflict have transformed Iran's missile program from a local deterrent into a long-range strategic weapon capable of threatening targets well outside the Middle East. Iran has reportedly developed new guidance systems and extended the range of its ballistic missiles significantly during the conflict period. This is a major security development for Western nations and their allies, shifting the threat calculus globally.

stories.title: Taiwan bans short-selling to stabilise AI stock market
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's government stepped in to ban short-selling (betting that stocks will fall) on its stock exchange after a sharp sell-off in AI and semiconductor stocks. Taiwan is home to TSMC, the world's most important chip manufacturer — the company that makes the chips powering AI globally. When Taiwan's tech market is in freefall severe enough to require emergency intervention, it signals real stress in global AI supply chains and investor sentiment. This directly contributed to last night's NASDAQ rout.

stories.title: UN talks on AI in warfare end with no binding rules agreed
stories.why_it_matters: United Nations talks aimed at establishing international rules around the use of AI in military operations wrapped up over the weekend without any binding agreement. Countries couldn't reach consensus on even basic guardrails for autonomous weapons systems — drones, targeting algorithms, and AI-driven battlefield decisions. Without agreed rules, there's nothing stopping nations from deploying AI weapons without human oversight, raising serious risks of miscalculation and accidental escalation in future conflicts.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, taking on Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2
stories.why_it_matters: Google dropped Gemini 4 Neon over the weekend, its latest AI model going head-to-head with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol. This is the cutting edge of the AI war between the world's biggest tech companies. For everyday users, these models can now handle far more complex reasoning, coding, and creative tasks than their predecessors. For investors, it confirms Google is staying competitive in the AI race despite the broader tech sell-off — relevant if you hold GOOG or GXAI.AX.

markets.summary: A rough session across the board. Last night in the US, the NASDAQ cratered 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% — a significant risk-off move driven by tech weakness and global uncertainty. The ASX followed suit today, falling 1.6%. Gold sold off sharply (-4.6%), which is unusual and suggests investors were selling assets to cover losses elsewhere. Oil was barely changed. The Aussie dollar slipped slightly to US$0.662.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Fell 1.6% today, dragged down by the Wall Street sell-off flowing through overnight.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Dropped 3.7% last night — a big move. Broad selling across all sectors.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Crashed 5.3% last night. Tech stocks were hammered, with AI and semiconductor names leading losses.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Barely moved despite the Iran-Bahrain escalation. Watch this — any further Middle East flare-up could push oil higher.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold fell sharply — unusual for a risk-off day. Likely means investors were selling gold to raise cash to cover losses in other positions.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar dipped slightly. Weak global risk appetite tends to push the AUD lower as investors flock to the US dollar.

politics.summary: Australian political and economic debate today is focused on the RBA's interest rate stance, Australia's diesel fuel vulnerability, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong flagging AI as a national security threat. Google also quietly pulled funding from 25 Aussie news outlets.

stories.title: Penny Wong to frame AI as a major foreign policy and national security challenge
stories.why_it_matters: Foreign Minister Penny Wong is set to deliver a major speech elevating AI to a top-tier foreign policy concern, arguing that AI-powered disinformation, autonomous weapons, and the geopolitical competition over AI chips poses a genuine national security risk for Australia. This signals Canberra is shifting from treating AI as a tech policy issue to treating it as a defence and diplomacy issue — expect more government scrutiny of AI investments and potentially new export controls or alliance commitments around chip supply chains.

stories.title: RBA under fire as divided board faces unemployment shock
stories.why_it_matters: New unemployment data has rattled confidence in the RBA's interest rate strategy, with reports suggesting the central bank may have raised rates too aggressively. The RBA board is reportedly divided on whether to hold, cut, or even raise further. For everyday Australians with mortgages, this matters enormously — a rate cut would mean lower repayments. For investors, rate cuts typically boost share prices and property values. Watch for the next RBA meeting for signals on direction.

stories.title: Australia's dangerous dependence on imported diesel — and what to do about it
stories.why_it_matters: A new report highlights that Australia holds less than 30 days of diesel reserves — well below the 90-day minimum recommended by the International Energy Agency. With almost all of our diesel imported, any disruption to Middle East shipping (like the Iran escalation this weekend) could cause fuel shortages and price spikes within weeks. The report argues Australia needs to urgently invest in domestic renewable fuel alternatives and strategic reserves. This affects transport costs, food prices, and supply chains for every Australian.

stories.title: Google cancels funding for 25 Australian news outlets
stories.why_it_matters: Google has abruptly cancelled its funding agreements with 25 Australian news organisations under the federal government's News Media Bargaining Code — the law designed to make tech giants pay for news content. The affected outlets span metro and regional Australia. This is a significant blow to Australian journalism funding and raises fresh questions about whether the Code is working as intended or whether Google is simply finding ways around it. The government may face pressure to strengthen the legislation.

ai.summary: AI was front and centre this weekend — Google launched a major new model, the UN failed to agree on AI weapons rules, protesters took to the streets in London, and Taiwan had to intervene in markets to stop an AI stock rout.

stories.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon — takes on Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol
stories.why_it_matters: Google released Gemini 4 Neon, its most advanced AI model yet, directly competing with Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 and OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Sol. In practical terms, these next-gen models can handle far more complex multi-step tasks — think writing full software applications, conducting legal research, or running autonomous business processes. The AI model race is now so fast-moving that a new generation drops every few months. Good news for GOOG holders — it shows Google isn't being left behind despite the recent Gemini struggles.

stories.title: UN talks on AI in warfare collapse with no binding rules
stories.why_it_matters: UN-led negotiations aimed at setting international limits on AI in warfare ended over the weekend without any binding agreement. Countries couldn't even agree on basic principles like requiring a human to approve lethal AI-driven decisions. The talks broke down largely along geopolitical lines. Without rules, autonomous AI weapons — drones that select and kill targets without human input — are effectively a free-for-all. This is a significant failure of international diplomacy with long-term consequences for global security.

stories.title: London protesters demand stricter AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: Protesters took to the streets in London over the weekend calling for tougher government oversight of AI systems, citing concerns about job losses, surveillance, deepfakes, and the use of AI in weapons. The demonstrations reflect growing public unease about how fast AI is being deployed without adequate safeguards. For investors, this signals a political environment where AI regulation is tightening — which could affect how quickly AI companies can roll out new products in Europe and the UK.

stories.title: Taiwan bans short-selling to rescue AI stock market
stories.why_it_matters: Taiwan's stock exchange regulators imposed an emergency ban on short-selling after its AI and semiconductor stocks — including TSMC, the world's dominant chip maker — went into freefall. The ban was introduced to prevent a self-reinforcing crash where short-sellers drive prices down further. This directly contributed to the global NASDAQ rout last night, as TSMC chips underpin virtually every major AI system. If Taiwan's semiconductor sector stays under pressure, it could slow the entire global AI buildout.

stories.title: America's AI chip policy has a critical gap, warns Washington Post
stories.why_it_matters: An opinion piece in the Washington Post argues that the US government's AI strategy has a critical blind spot: it focuses heavily on restricting China's access to advanced chips, but lacks a coherent plan to actually build and secure America's own chip manufacturing capacity. The concern is that export controls without domestic investment just slows everyone down, rather than giving the US a durable lead. This debate has real implications for investors in AI stocks — chip supply constraints are a key risk for the whole sector.

sport.summary: The NRL Grand Final is done — Roosters edged the Knights 19-18 in a thriller at Accor Stadium. There's also a big surf title for a 14-year-old Australian, and Jannik Sinner's Australian Open participation is in serious doubt.

stories.title: Roosters win 2026 NRL Grand Final 19-18 over Knights in a classic
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters claimed the 2026 NRL premiership with a heart-stopping 19-18 victory over the Newcastle Knights at Accor Stadium on Sunday. One point in it at the final whistle — it doesn't get tighter than that. The Knights came agonisingly close to their first title in decades. As your NRL Grand Final result, that's the season done and dusted.

stories.title: Leihani Zoric, 14, becomes women's world surfing champion
stories.why_it_matters: 14-year-old Leihani Zoric has made history by becoming the youngest women's world surfing champion ever. The result is a stunning breakthrough — at 14, she's beaten professionals many years her senior to claim the top title in women's professional surfing. Given the Gold Coast's surf culture, this is a story worth celebrating locally. Keep an eye on this name for years to come.

stories.title: Jannik Sinner's Australian Open participation in serious doubt
stories.why_it_matters: World number one Jannik Sinner is facing a race against time to be fit for the Australian Open after confirming a knee injury with three possible treatment options — ranging from rest and conservative management through to surgery. If he requires surgery, he almost certainly misses the Australian Open in January. Sinner won the AO last year and was the heavy favourite to defend his title. His absence would blow the men's draw wide open.

stories.title: 2026 AFL Draft — club-by-club takeaways
stories.why_it_matters: The 2026 AFL Draft has concluded, with Zero Hanger providing a full breakdown of which clubs won and lost on draft day. The draft is where AFL clubs build their future — the picks made now will determine which clubs are competitive in 3-5 years. No specific article text was available, but if you follow AFL, the full club-by-club analysis is worth a read.
